description: ¡Hola! Soy Paulina Carrasco, emprendedora en innovación y colidero de JIMCP | Humanity Beyond Earth para NASA Space Apps 2026. Investigaremos lugares de la Tierra similares a entornos lunares y marcianos usando datos abiertos, IA y mapas. Somos un equipo intergeneracional con experiencia en software, ciencia de datos, mecatrónica y formación espacial juvenil. Buscamos personas en geología, astronomía, GIS y teledetección, con curiosidad y ganas de colaborar. ¡Súmate a explorar!
summary:
Mission Mirror  turns a complex space exploration question into an actionable decision: Where on Earth should we test a technology before taking it to the Moon or Mars?

We developed a platform that compares extraterrestrial sites with terrestrial analogs using scientific and geospatial data, evaluating variables such as elevation, slope, roughness, and terrain relief. The tool not only identifies the most similar locations, but also shows how representative they are and the limitations of each comparison.

This matters because no place on Earth can perfectly replicate another world. Mission Mirror makes those differences visible and helps design more rigorous, transparent, and reproducible field tests, reducing uncertainty before a mission and enabling better decisions about where, how, and under what conditions to test technologies for space exploration.
details:
Mission Mirror is an interactive tool for identifying and evaluating locations on Earth that can serve as analogs for lunar terrain, with the goal of supporting the design of tests for technologies intended for future space missions.
What does it do and how does it work?

The system starts from real topographic data. For the Moon, we use LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) data from the lunar south pole, and for Earth, we use Copernicus DEM GLO-30. The prototype analyzes areas of approximately 3 × 3 km and brings lunar and terrestrial surfaces to a common analysis scale.

For each area, it calculates comparable terrain characteristics, mainly:

  • slope, including P50 and P90 percentiles;
  • terrain roughness;
  • local relief;
  • valid data coverage.

Based on these variables, Mission Mirror calculates a relative similarity distance and generates a ranking of terrestrial candidates. It does not provide a “similarity percentage,” because we believe that such a figure could create a false sense of precision. The tool keeps the individual metrics visible so users can understand why one location ranks higher than another.

The interface allows users to select a lunar area, explore the terrestrial regions analyzed, view the best candidates, compare the Moon and Earth metric by metric, and export results in GeoJSON and CSV formats. It also includes sensitivity tests and controls to evaluate how stable the ranking remains under reasonable changes in the parameters.

In addition to topography, we incorporated contextual information on temperature, geological composition, seismic activity, and volcanism, using open data sources. These variables are displayed as context and are not combined with the topographic score, avoiding the misleading treatment of data with different scales or scientific meanings as if they were equivalent.

What benefits does it offer?

Mission Mirror transforms multiple scientific datasets into a visual and understandable decision-support tool. Instead of selecting an Earth site only because it has historically been used as an analog, the platform enables a quantitative comparison between its characteristics and those of a specific lunar area.

This can help researchers and engineers:

  • identify relevant terrestrial candidates;
  • understand exactly which characteristics match and which do not;
  • compare different alternatives using a common methodology;
  • recognize the limitations of an analog before conducting a field test;
  • document and reproduce the site-selection process.

What is the expected impact?

No place on Earth fully reproduces the conditions of the Moon or Mars. Therefore, the value of Mission Mirror is not in declaring that one location is “identical,” but in making explicit which part of the environment we are reproducing and which part we are not.

Its potential impact is to support the design of more informed, transparent, and reproducible terrestrial experiments before technologies are tested in extraterrestrial environments. This can reduce uncertainty during early planning stages and allow the selection of an analog site to be supported by quantifiable evidence.

The current prototype is exploratory: it does not certify terrain suitability for a rover and does not constitute NASA validation. This limitation is explicitly communicated within the application itself.

Tools and technologies used

The geospatial processing and analysis were developed primarily in Python, using libraries such as NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, and Rasterio. We also used Requests to access open data sources and Pytest to test the methodology.

The web application was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Leaflet for map visualization. The project and its source code were managed in GitHub, and the web demonstration is published through GitHub Pages.

No specialized hardware was used as part of the prototype; Mission Mirror is a software-based solution built around geospatial data processing and web visualization.

In what way is the project creative?

The creative element of Mission Mirror is not simply displaying maps, but transforming the search for a planetary analog intoInstead of starting with the question, “What is the best terrestrial analog?”, Mission Mirror starts with a specific area on the Moon and asks:

Which place on Earth best reproduces the characteristics we need to test, and what limitations will that comparison have?

The system separates similarity, context, and limitations; allows different regions to be explored using the same methodology; and makes uncertainty visible instead of hiding it behind a single score.

Factors considered by the team

During development, we paid particular attention to data quality and resolution, differences between lunar and terrestrial coordinate systems, the need to compare surfaces at a common scale, valid coverage within each analysis window, and the inherent limitations of DEM data.

We also considered that topographic similarity alone does not represent all the conditions required for a mission. Factors such as soil properties, small rocks, traction, site accessibility, and operational permits still require additional information or field validation.

For this reason, we designed Mission Mirror so that its results are interpretable and traceable, showing both where a match exists and where that match stops being valid.
